thread.title: TCAT Receives 5 Buses to Ease Transit Shortage
thread.title_full: TCAT Receives 5 Buses to Ease Transit Shortage

author: world today news
title: TCAT Receives 5 Buses to Ease Transit Shortage
text:
Facing ongoing reliability issues, TCAT is adding five donated hybrid buses to its fleet in an effort to enhance public transit services. This article details how the addition of these used hybrid buses is expected to provide a much-needed boost to the TCAT’s operations and improve the experience of riders. Learn about the factors behind this decision and how this impacts the future of public transportation in the region.
TCAT Bolsters Fleet with Donated Hybrid Buses Amidst Reliability Concerns Addressing a Critical Shortage Ithaca, N.Y. — Tompkins Consolidated Area Transit (TCAT) is set to deploy five donated hybrid buses in Tompkins county in the coming weeks, a move aimed at alleviating a persistent shortage of usable vehicles. The buses, previously part of the Capital District Transit Authority’s fleet serving Albany, N.Y., were retired by the agency after 15 years of service and later gifted to TCAT.
The acquisition comes at a crucial time for TCAT, which has faced challenges in meeting service demands following the decommissioning of seven electric buses due to significant reliability issues. The addition of these hybrid buses is expected to provide much-needed stability to the transit system.
Impact on Riders TCAT General Manager Matthew rosenbloom-Jones emphasized the positive impact this addition will have on riders. For riders this means less breakdowns and fewer cancelled trips, Rosenbloom-Jones stated in an email. This improvement is notably significant given the recent struggles with the electric bus fleet.
Fleet Expansion and Future Acquisitions With the introduction of these hybrid buses, TCAT’s usable fleet will total 34 vehicles.Rosenbloom-Jones noted that the agency has not received a new full-size bus in four years, excluding the problematic electric buses. However, the situation is set to improve with further acquisitions planned for this year.
Five diesel buses are slated for delivery. Six battery electric buses are also expected. Two additional hybrid buses are currently being ordered. Rosenbloom-Jones stressed the importance of timely fleet replacement to prevent breakdowns and service disruptions.
Legislative Approval and Bus Details The Tompkins County Legislature formally accepted the donated buses during its April 1 meeting,following their initial arrival in November.As of now,two of the five buses are already in service,while the remaining three are undergoing state inspection.
According to county documents, all five hybrid buses were manufactured in 2010 and have odometer readings averaging just over 600,000 miles. Despite their age, they are expected to provide valuable service to TCAT.
Extended Lifespan and Limited Service While the buses are beyond the 12-year lifespan defined by the Federal Transit Administration , Rosenbloom-Jones expressed confidence in their condition.
These buses are already two years beyond their 12-year lifespan that is defined by the Federal Transit Administration. That being said, they are in excellent shape and have been well cared for and will likely be able to be used by TCAT in limited service for the next few years.
Matthew Rosenbloom-jones, TCAT General Manager
The hybrid buses are manufactured by Gillig , a different company than Proterra , which supplied the electric buses that were ultimately deemed unusable.Hybrid technology is generally considered more established and reliable compared to fully electric bus technology, offering greater versatility.
Electric Bus Troubles and Proterra Bankruptcy The decision to decommission the electric buses followed the bankruptcy of Proterra in 2023, which severely hampered TCAT’s ability to obtain replacement parts. The electric buses, introduced in 2021, were pulled from service after only three years.
Government Collaboration At a recent meeting, county legislators expressed their gratitude to both TCAT and the Capital District Transit Authority for facilitating the bus transfer. Transit agencies receiving federal aid can freely transfer vehicles purchased with those funds between each other, provided the vehicles are fully paid off. TCAT will not be responsible for any monthly payments on the donated buses.
County Legislator Randy Brown highlighted the collaborative effort involved:
I think this is an example of something were the government is doing the right thing. We worked together and solved a problem.
Randy Brown, county Legislator
